# Diagnosing a Hyundai Elantra That Cranks But Doesn't Start

When a vehicle like a 2013 Hyundai Elantra turns over smoothly but refuses to ignite, it presents a classic "no fuel" or "no spark" scenario. Since the dashboard lights and gear indicator are functioning normally, you can confidently rule out a total battery failure. While a weak alternator might eventually leave you stranded after driving, a completely dead battery usually results in silence rather than cranking. If Napa Auto Parts confirmed the battery voltage is within spec, your focus must shift to the fuel delivery system or ignition timing.

The symptom described—"it just seems like there's no gas getting to it"—points toward a few specific failure points common in this model year. The most frequent culprit is the fuel pump relay. In many Hyundai models from this era, the relay sits under the hood near the battery. It acts as an electric switch that sends 12 volts to the fuel pump when the key is turned to the "start" position. If the coil inside the relay has burned out or the contacts are corroded, the engine cranks (because the starter motor gets power through a separate circuit) but the fuel pump never engages.

To verify this without immediate disassembly, listen closely for the faint whirring sound of the fuel pump priming when you turn the key to the "ON" position before attempting to start. If there is silence, check the relay by swapping it with an identical one from another circuit, such as the A/C or horn relay. This is a safe troubleshooting step because these components are standardized across the vehicle's fuse box. If the swapped relay resolves the issue, you have found your fault.

Another possibility involves the fuel pump itself. The pump is located inside the rear of the gas tank, secured by a metal ring that must be removed to access it. Accessing this component requires dropping the rear seat cushion and removing the trim panel behind the back seat. Once exposed, the entire fuel tank assembly often needs to be lowered from the chassis. This is labor-intensive work that many independent mechanics prefer to avoid unless absolutely necessary. Given your vehicle is still under an extended warranty, attempting a DIY repair on the pump or its wiring harness risks voiding coverage. The safest path is a professional tow and diagnostic scan at an authorized dealer to confirm if the Pump Control Module (PCM) is sending the correct signal.

There are also less common but critical checks. Sometimes the fuel pump fuse blows due to a short in the wiring, cutting power before it reaches the relay. A quick visual inspection of the main fuse box under the dashboard can rule this out. Additionally, ensure that the gear selector is actually locked in Park or Neutral; while modern Elantras have safety interlocks that allow cranking in Drive or Reverse, some vehicles may still inhibit fuel injection if the transmission range sensor detects an invalid state.

Since the car is covered by warranty, towing it to a certified service center is the most prudent move. They can perform a live data scan of the PCM to see if fuel pressure readings are being reported as zero. If the system reports no signal from the pump circuit, they will likely replace the relay or fuse box module first before attempting tank removal. This approach minimizes labor costs and ensures any hidden wiring faults are caught early.
